title: Proportionality and Legitimate Expectation in Administrative Law

content.overview: Proportionality is a standard of judicial review that asks whether an administrative measure is suitable, necessary and not excessive in relation to a legitimate aim. In Indian administrative law it is applied with varying intensity depending on the rights engaged and the nature of the power. Legitimate expectation is a related but distinct doctrine protecting procedural or substantive expectations generated by a public authority's representation or settled practice, subject to overriding public interest.
content.glance: Identify the legitimate aim, the means chosen, whether less restrictive alternatives existed, and whether the burden on the affected person is excessive. Keep proportionality analysis separate from legitimate-expectation claims based on representation or past practice.
content.study:
Core idea: proportionality reviews the relationship between ends and means. A measure that pursues a legitimate aim may still fail if it is unsuitable, unnecessary or disproportionate in its impact on the affected interest.

Structure of the inquiry: Courts commonly examine (1) whether the aim is legitimate, (2) whether the means are rationally connected to that aim, (3) whether a less restrictive means would achieve the aim, and (4) whether the overall balance between the benefit and the burden is fair. The intensity of this inquiry varies with the rights and interests at stake.

Relationship to reasonableness: Traditional reasonableness review asks whether the decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it. Proportionality is a more structured and sometimes more intensive inquiry into means and ends. Indian courts have drawn on both approaches depending on context.

Legitimate expectation (related but distinct): A legitimate expectation may arise from an express promise, a regular practice, or a published policy. It primarily protects procedural fairness (a hearing before departure) and, in limited circumstances, may support substantive protection, always subject to statutory power and overriding public interest. Do not collapse proportionality into legitimate expectation or vice versa.

Judicial review limits: Proportionality does not turn the court into the primary decision-maker. The court tests the legality of the balance struck; it does not substitute its own policy preference where the authority has acted within lawful bounds.

Current-law framing: Ground the analysis in the Constitution (especially Articles 14 and 21 where engaged) and the specific statute creating the administrative power. Do not treat the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 as the source of proportionality or legitimate-expectation doctrine; evidence provisions apply only when proof issues arise.

sections.heading: Meaning and Purpose of Proportionality
sections.body: Proportionality is a structured standard for reviewing whether administrative means are suitable, necessary and not excessive relative to a legitimate aim. Its purpose is to prevent unnecessary or excessive interference with rights and interests while respecting the authority's primary role in policy and administration.

sections.heading: Steps of the Proportionality Inquiry
sections.body: Identify the aim claimed by the authority and test whether it is legitimate under the governing law. Examine whether the means are rationally connected to that aim. Ask whether a less restrictive alternative would achieve the aim. Finally assess whether the overall burden on the affected person is disproportionate to the benefit pursued.

sections.heading: Intensity of Review and Relationship to Reasonableness
sections.body: The intensity of proportionality review depends on the rights engaged and the nature of the power. Where fundamental rights or severe adverse consequences are involved, courts may scrutinise the balance more closely. Traditional reasonableness review remains relevant and should not be treated as identical to structured proportionality in every case.

sections.heading: Legitimate Expectation Distinguished
sections.body: Legitimate expectation arises from a representation, settled practice or published policy of a public authority. It primarily secures procedural fairness before a departure from the expectation and, in limited cases, may support substantive protection subject to overriding public interest and statutory limits. It is a distinct doctrine from proportionality and should be pleaded and analysed separately.

sections.heading: Remedies
sections.body: Where a measure fails proportionality or a legitimate-expectation claim succeeds on the facts, relief may include quashing, remittal for a lawful decision, or a direction to afford a hearing before departure from the expectation. The precise remedy depends on the statutory scheme and the nature of the defect.

examples.title: Excessive blanket ban
examples.body: An authority imposes a complete prohibition on an activity to address a limited risk that could be controlled by targeted conditions. The issue is whether the means are necessary and proportionate to the legitimate aim of risk control.

examples.title: Suitable but not least restrictive
examples.body: A regulator chooses a highly restrictive measure that achieves the statutory aim, but a clearly available less restrictive alternative would achieve the same aim with far less impact on the affected persons. The analysis should test necessity and overall balance.

examples.title: Expectation from published policy
examples.body: A department publishes a policy stating that a class of applications will be processed under stated criteria, then departs from that policy without notice or hearing. The issue is legitimate expectation and procedural fairness, not automatically a proportionality failure.

hypotheticals.question: Is every restrictive administrative measure disproportionate?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. First identify the legitimate aim and the statutory power. Test suitability, necessity and overall balance. A restrictive measure may still be proportionate if it is the least restrictive effective means and the balance is fair in context.

hypotheticals.question: A person relied on a past practice of the authority. Is that enough for substantive relief?
hypotheticals.analysis: Not automatically. Identify whether a legitimate expectation arose from representation or practice, whether procedural fairness required a hearing before departure, and whether overriding public interest or statutory limits justify the change. Keep this analysis separate from structured proportionality.

distinctions.title: Proportionality vs traditional reasonableness
distinctions.left: Proportionality is a structured means-ends inquiry (suitability, necessity, balance).
distinctions.right: Traditional reasonableness asks whether the decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it.

rows.left: Step-wise analysis of aim, means and burden.
May be more intensive where rights are engaged.

distinctions.title: Proportionality vs legitimate expectation
distinctions.left: Proportionality tests the balance between aim and means of a measure.
distinctions.right: Legitimate expectation protects reliance on a representation, practice or policy.

rows.right: Promise, practice or published policy generating an expectation.

rows.left: Quash or remit if means are excessive or unnecessary.
rows.right: Hearing before departure; limited substantive protection subject to public interest.

misconceptions.trap: Any strict regulation is automatically disproportionate.
misconceptions.correction: Strictness alone is not fatal; the measure must be tested for suitability, necessity and overall balance against a legitimate aim.

misconceptions.trap: Proportionality and legitimate expectation are the same doctrine.
misconceptions.correction: They are related but distinct: one is a means-ends review standard; the other protects expectations generated by representation or practice.
Proportionality and legitimate expectation arise from constitutional and administrative-law principles; evidence law is relevant only to evidentiary questions.

cases.name: CBSE v Aditya Bandopadhyay
cases.facts: The case concerned access to evaluated answer-books and the scope of information rights under the applicable information-law framework.
cases.issue: What is the scope of the right to access information in the examination context under the governing statute?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examined the statutory information-access framework and the balance between transparency and other protected interests on the facts before it.
cases.holding: The Court disposed of the appeal by applying the governing statutory and constitutional standards to the information-access claim.
cases.relevance: Authority already present in the topic file; primarily an information-access decision. Use only for propositions actually decided; case-law verification remains a separate gate.

cases.name: Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v CIC
cases.facts: The case concerned a request for personal information of a public servant and the exemptions under the information-law framework.
cases.issue: When is personal information of a public servant exempt from disclosure under the governing statute?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examined the statutory exemptions relating to personal information and the conditions for disclosure on the record before it.
cases.holding: The Court applied the statutory exemption framework to the information request under challenge.
cases.relevance: Authority already present in the topic file; primarily an RTI/personal-information decision. Do not treat it as a general proportionality authority without verified proposition mapping.

cases.name: CPIO v Subhash Chandra Agarwal
cases.facts: The case concerned disclosure claims involving high constitutional offices and the interaction of transparency with other institutional interests.
cases.issue: How should courts balance transparency claims with other protected interests under the information-law and constitutional framework?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examined the statutory and constitutional balance between access to information and competing institutional or privacy interests.
cases.holding: The Court applied that balancing framework to the disclosure claims under challenge.
cases.relevance: Authority already present in the topic file; useful for structured balancing discussion but not a substitute for classic proportionality authorities. Verification remains a separate gate.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a proportionality challenge be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the power and the legitimate aim. II. Test suitability of the means. III. Test necessity (less restrictive alternatives). IV. Assess overall balance between benefit and burden. V. If legitimate expectation is also pleaded, analyse it separately. VI. Identify the appropriate remedy.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should written submissions on proportionality contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Set out the enabling power and the aim claimed; identify the restrictive means and their impact; apply suitability, necessity and balance; address any less restrictive alternative; keep legitimate-expectation arguments distinct if raised; and seek only the relief supported by the governing law and record.
